Servetus
sẽr-vē´tŭs
n. (Michael Servetus, 1511–1553, Spanish physician and anti-trinitarian, burned at Geneva)
Latinised form of Miguel Serveto. He published On the Errors of the Trinity at twenty, and was condemned by Rome and by the Reformed alike before his death at Geneva.

Biblical Definition

Servetus denied the Trinity, holding the Son and the Spirit to be modes or manifestations rather than distinct Persons. The doctrine he denied is stated in the baptismal formula, one name and three: “baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost” (Mat 28:19); in the Word who “was with God, and… was God” (John 1:1); in the benediction that names all three (2Co 13:14); and at the Jordan, where the Son is baptised, the Spirit descends, and the Father speaks (Mat 3:16–17). His execution is the permanent stain on the Reformed record and is dealt with plainly below.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no entry for Servetus; his definition of heresy is the relevant one: a fundamental error in religion, or an error of opinion respecting some fundamental doctrine of religion.

expand to see more

HERESY, n. A fundamental error in religion, or an error of opinion respecting some fundamental doctrine of religion.

2. Heresy, in law, is an offense against Christianity, consisting in a denial of some of its essential doctrines, publicly avowed and obstinately maintained.

Key Scripture

Mat 28:19 — "Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:"

John 1:1 — "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God."

2Co 13:14 — "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all. Amen."

Mat 3:16 — "And Jesus, when he was baptized, went up straightway out of the water: and, lo, the heavens were opened unto him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and lighting upon him:"

Luk 9:55 — "But he turned, and rebuked them, and said, Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of."

Modern Corruption

The case is used to dismiss Calvin entirely or is defended as a necessity of the age, and neither answer is honest.

expand to see more

Two dishonest treatments of Servetus circulate, and this dictionary should hold neither. The first uses the burning to void everything Calvin wrote, as though a man's exegesis of Romans were refuted by his conduct in 1553. The second defends the execution as the ordinary practice of the age — true as history, since Rome had already condemned him and would have done the same, and the city council rather than Calvin passed the sentence — and then treats that context as a justification. It is an explanation and not a justification, and the distinction matters.

The plain judgment is that it was wrong: wrong because the civil sword has no jurisdiction over heresy, which is the very principle the Reformed later came to hold and which the Second London Confession states in its chapter on liberty of conscience; and wrong because the Lord had already answered the question when two disciples proposed fire for a village that refused Him, and He turned and rebuked them, saying, ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of (Luk 9:55). Servetus's doctrine was fatal error and the church was right to refuse it. The fire was not the church's to light.

The doctrine itself is worth stating, because anti-trinitarianism keeps returning under new names. Servetus's objection was that Trinity is unbiblical language, which is true of the word and false of the content: one God, and the Father sends, the Son is sent, and the Spirit proceeds; each is called God, and they are distinguished in the same sentences that unite them. The vocabulary was framed precisely because men kept finding ways to say God while meaning something less, and the creeds are the church's record of every such attempt and its answer.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek onoma (G3686), name — singular in Matthew 28:19 with three genitives; hupostasis (G5287), person, substance; hairesis (G139), heresy, a chosen party.

expand to see more

Greek eis to onoma (G3686) — into the name; Matthew 28:19 — one name, three Persons.

Greek hupostasis (G5287) — person; Hebrews 1:3, the express image of his person.

Greek hairesis (G139) — heresy, sect; Galatians 5:20, 2 Peter 2:1, Titus 3:10.

Usage

"“In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost” — one name, three."

"“Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of” — said to disciples who proposed fire."

"“A man that is an heretick… reject” — the apostolic penalty, and it is not the stake."
